how_it_wins:
The table will look at the commander, decide you are the Yawgmoth deck, and point their removal at him. Let them.

Three of your four verified kills never name him, and the fourth is the slow one. His job is cards. That ability costs no mana at all, so it runs through a tax, through a lock, and at instant speed on somebody else's end step.

He shows up on turn four in 7,220 of 10,000 goldfished games without any help from you. So spend your first four turns building a board for him to eat rather than digging for him.

Then win with something he was never part of. Two of your kills are unbounded — stack 009 funds itself with Treasure, stack 011 pays nothing at all and gains you a life a lap. Stack 012 is lethal precisely because it stops. Stack 010 is real too, and it is the one that spends a resource from outside the loop: your library, at 39 activations of the 59 you get.

All four take four opponents from 40 to 0 at the same moment. So never aim a kill at a player. You are not killing a seat, you are ending the game, and the seat you were annoyed with leaves with everybody else.

Here is the gap you actually pilot around. Your enabler layers are enormous — by turn 10 you have a drain 82.4% of the time, a free sacrifice outlet 77.9%, renewable fodder 73.6%, an ignition source 73.1%. The named kills read tiny beside that: 1.1%, 0.5%, 6.9% and 4.6% unassisted. Read those one at a time and never add them up.

Do not read the split as fragility. Read it as your instructions. The machine will be running; your turns go to hunting the one missing card. That is what five tutors are for, and a tutor is what carries the Exquisite Blood kill from 6.9% to 42.5% — so never cast one for value.

A wrath is not what beats you. Bastion of Remembrance, Zulaport Cutthroat, Blood Artist and The Meathook Massacre all get paid when your creatures die, and Gravecrawler and Reassembling Skeleton rebuild cheaper than anyone at the table.

What beats you is a permanent you cannot remove. One card in the 99 destroys a noncreature permanent an opponent controls, and it only reaches enchantments. So stop planning to answer the hate and pick the kill that dodges it — Exquisite Blood needs no graveyard, no outlet and no recursion.

Deploy in the order that costs you least when it gets answered, and put the drain down last, because the drain is the piece that tells the table what you are. Present the assembly when their mana is spent. Say bracket 4 at Rule 0 — four Game Changers and eleven two-card infinite records force it — then go play exactly the deck you just described.

combo_lines.002: The clause is “up to one target creature”, and targets are locked in when the ability is activated (CR 115.1c) — the Insect the Nest is about to make does not yet exist to be chosen. Protection from Humans keeps Yawgmoth off his own list (CR 702.16b). So the moment the opponent's creature is dead, every legal target is one of your own tokens: two bodies leave, one comes back. The holding: this engine draws cards and then stops. It is not a kill, and no ordering makes it one.
combo_lines.003: Three permissions, and not a restriction among them. You choose which creature pays “Sacrifice another creature” (CR 601.2h), “up to one target” permits choosing none (CR 115.6), and a leaves-the-battlefield trigger looks back at the board as it was (CR 603.10a). Nothing here can take Zulaport Cutthroat away from you against your will. He survives every iteration and is spent as the deliberate final sacrifice, where his own trigger banks the seventh drain. The holding: seven drains, and the table lives through them.
combo_lines.004: Four words decide the case. Blood Artist reads “target player loses 1 life” — one seat per trigger, chosen as the trigger goes on the stack — where the drains that end games read each opponent. The engine also finishes by eating its own payoff: protection bars the commander as a target and “another creature” bars him as the sacrifice, so the Artist is the last legal thing left to point at. The holding: eight triggers, eight life, against a pod holding 160. The arithmetic divides by four and never recovers.
combo_lines.005: CR 119.9 is the clause, and it is a small one: an event that gains you 0 life is not a life-gain event at all. An Insect killed by its own -1/-1 counter dies at toughness 0, so South Wind Avatar's dies-trigger resolves for nothing and the second ability never fires. The holding: eight dies-triggers, seven drains. The Avatar's 4 toughness is what does the real work here, absorbing counters that a 1/1 drainer could not take.
combo_lines.006: CR 122.6 is broader than it first reads: a reference to putting counters on an object covers an object given counters as it enters, not only counters placed on something already sitting there. Persist names no player, so 122.6a makes you the one placing it — which is precisely what Nest of Scarabs asks for. The holding: the Nest triggers and you get an Insect, even though the returned Fume Spitter is back in the graveyard before that trigger reaches the stack. It had already triggered.
combo_lines.008: Savour the order of operations. A cost is paid after the ability is already the topmost object on the stack (CR 602.2a into 601.2h), so the trigger the sacrifice causes lands above it and resolves first. One activation paid with a token therefore pays Mirkwood Bats twice: once for the sacrifice, once for the creation two resolutions later. One caveat for the record — a token killed by its own counter is put into the graveyard by the game rather than sacrificed by you (CR 704.5f), and pays the Bats on creation only.
combo_lines.009: The elegant clause is CR 113.6f: an ability that modifies which zones its own card may be cast from functions in that zone. Gravecrawler's permission is therefore live in the graveyard every iteration, its Zombie condition met by Warren Soultrader, whom “another creature” keeps permanently out of the loop. Each Treasure is an artifact and not a creature, so it funds the recast without restriction. The holding: the loop pays for itself, one drain a lap, and nothing on this board brings it to an end.
combo_lines.010: CR 704.5q is the crux — a permanent holding both a +1/+1 and a -1/-1 counter loses one of each to state-based actions. So the commander's counter does not shrink an undying body. It strips the +1/+1 that undying left behind and re-arms the creature to die again. The holding: the alternation is real, and the loop is finite, because the draw is mandatory. It needs 39 activations against the 59 the library permits, a margin of 20. One trap the record is explicit about: Viscera Seer's own sacrifice places no counter, and only the commander's counter can strip an undying return, so a mid-loop activation costs a body that cannot be re-armed.
combo_lines.011: One line of rules text carries the whole thing. Phyrexian Altar's ability needs no target and could add mana, so it is a mana ability (CR 605.1a) and never uses the stack (CR 605.3b) — the {B} is in the pool before anyone receives priority, and there is nothing to respond to. Sacrificing Gravecrawler refunds exactly the mana that recasts him, with Carrion Feeder holding the Zombie condition and never being the sacrifice. The holding: unbounded, and free — each lap costs nothing and gains you a life.
combo_lines.012: Counsel's favourite kind of question: the loop is mandatory — neither card says “may” — so does the game simply end in a draw? No, and CR 732.1b is why. A draw requires a sequence that could be repeated indefinitely, and this one cannot, because every cycle takes a life from every opponent. There is a way to stop, which is all CR 104.4b asks. The holding: drain 40 takes all four opponents to 0, state-based actions are checked before the resulting triggers reach the stack, and they leave together (CR 704.5a). You are still there, so you win (CR 104.2a).

card_roles.Yawgmoth, Thran Physician: Cast him to draw, not to win — the ability costs no mana at all, so run it at instant speed on the turn before yours and convert spare bodies into cards. By the time the table finally answers him you should be several cards up and holding a kill he was never part of.
card_roles.Nest of Scarabs: Every counter you place becomes a body, so point the commander's counters at their creatures when you need the board clear and at your own when you need fodder. Count by creatures touched, not counters placed — one proliferate across three counter-bearing creatures hands you three Insects.
card_roles.Mirkwood Bats: Get it down before you start converting tokens, not after: one commander activation paid with a token pays this drain twice, once going out and once coming back. Its 2/3 body also absorbs two counters and lives, which buys you activations a 1/1 cannot.
card_roles.Ayara, First of Locthwain: Play her the moment your first three lands are black and let every black creature that follows chip the whole table. Keep one spare black body back for her tap-to-draw rather than feeding everything to the commander.
card_roles.Bastion of Remembrance: Treat this as a combo piece, not a value enchantment — it is the drain three of your verified kills route through, so resolve it on the turn you mean to convert rather than the turn you draw it. It also hands you a free Soldier to eat on arrival.
card_roles.Zulaport Cutthroat: A drain on a body that slots into any recursion kill, and nothing can force you to eat him. Sacrifice him last and on purpose: his own trigger sees his death and banks one more drain.
card_roles.Blood Artist: He hits one seat per trigger where your real finishers hit all four, so play him for value and never tutor for him as the kill. He is still the best thing to have on the battlefield when somebody wraths.
card_roles.South Wind Avatar: Deathtouch keeps him alive on defence and his toughness soaks counters, but the line that matters is the second one — gain a life, every opponent loses one. Put him beside Exquisite Blood and stop looking for anything else.
card_roles.Exquisite Blood: Your fastest kill and the only one that touches no graveyard and needs no outlet, so reach for this shape the moment somebody lands hate on the rest of the deck. The pair comes together on a mean turn 5.301, so play toward it early rather than treating it as a late-game plan.
card_roles.Marauding Blight-Priest: The same each-opponent lifegain trigger on a cheaper body — your second and third shot at the Exquisite Blood kill. Deploy him early, while the table still reads him as a 2/2 that does nothing.
card_roles.Starscape Cleric: Cheap, flies, and carries the lifegain drain. Buy the Offspring copy whenever the mana is spare: two bodies with that trigger means the table loses two life for every life you gain.
card_roles.The Meathook Massacre: Cast it when your board is the one that profits — your creatures dying drains each opponent, theirs dying gains you life, and X scales to whatever has been deployed. This is the wipe you want to be holding, not the one you fear.
card_roles.Grave Pact: Your only repeatable edict and your answer to a creature you cannot target: every sacrifice you were making anyway now costs each opponent a body. Land it before the protected threat arrives, not after.
card_roles.Gravecrawler: The one slot with no substitute — two unbounded kills route through him. Keep a second Zombie on the battlefield at all times so his recast permission stays live, and never let the loop eat that Zombie.
card_roles.Warren Soultrader: A Zombie who turns each sacrifice into a Treasure, and that Treasure exactly pays Gravecrawler's next cast. He satisfies the Zombie condition himself, so sacrifice anything on the board except him.
card_roles.Phyrexian Altar: Your best engine mana: sacrifice for any colour, and it never uses the stack, so nobody gets a window to respond. With Gravecrawler and a spare Zombie the loop costs you nothing to run.
card_roles.Pitiless Plunderer: Every other creature you lose becomes a Treasure, which turns a board wipe into a pile of mana. Four mana looks steep right up until the turn you sacrifice five things.
card_roles.Ashnod's Altar: Free outlet and two colorless whenever you need a body gone at instant speed. Know the limit before you rely on it: colorless does not recast Gravecrawler, so use it for outlet work and bulk mana, never as the loop's fuel.
card_roles.Phyrexian Tower: An outlet, two black mana and a land drop in one slot. Save the activation for the turn the mana matters — you only get it once a turn.
card_roles.Carrion Feeder: One mana, a free outlet, and a Zombie — that last word is why he can stand in the recursion loop and hold Gravecrawler's permission open. He cannot block, so plan your defence elsewhere.
card_roles.Viscera Seer: One mana for a free outlet that filters every draw. Keep her out of the Mikaeus loop mid-stream — her sacrifice places no counter, so it costs a body you cannot re-arm. Save her for the finish.
card_roles.Woe Strider: A free outlet, a Goat to feed it on arrival, and escape from your own graveyard after the table wipes. Three jobs for three mana, and you will use all three.
card_roles.Yahenni, Undying Partisan: The outlet that lives through your own sweepers — sacrifice anything and she is indestructible for the turn. She is also a legal undying body under Mikaeus.
card_roles.Blasting Station: A free outlet that closes from a board no drain can reach, and it untaps every time a creature enters, which with your token production is constantly. Sequence your tokens into it and keep pulling the trigger.
card_roles.Reassembling Skeleton: Pay two, get a body, forever. Hold the mana for it on any turn you have nothing better to do — this is the fodder that never runs out.
card_roles.Butcher Ghoul: A Zombie that dies twice by itself and switches on Gravecrawler's recast for a single black. Under Mikaeus he is a legal alternation body.
card_roles.Geralf's Messenger: Three black pips buys a Zombie that has to be killed twice and takes 2 off a seat every time it arrives. Cast him on a turn where a tapped body costs you nothing.
card_roles.Stitcher's Supplier: One mana for a Zombie that fills your graveyard coming in and going out. Play it on turn one — your recursion suite wants targets more than you want the 1/1.
card_roles.Bitterblossom: Two mana for a body every upkeep, at a life apiece, for the rest of the game — and it keeps producing while you hold up interaction. Play it on turn two every single time.
card_roles.Grave Titan: Ten power across three bodies, and two more Zombies every time it attacks. This is how an emptied board becomes an engine again, and it is the best thing in your graveyard to reanimate.
card_roles.Sedgemoor Witch: Ward makes her expensive to answer and every instant or sorcery you cast hands you a Pest. Those Pests gain you life when they die, which your lifegain drains are watching for.
card_roles.Black Market Connections: Take the mode the board is short of every first main phase — a Treasure, a card, or a 3/2 — and pay the life without flinching. That flexibility beats a fixed draw engine in a deck that needs a different resource every turn.
card_roles.Necropotence: Life is your cheapest resource in a deck whose loops finish at 80, so spend it hard. Decide how many you want before you start paying: the cards arrive at your end step, and a turn spent overpaying is a turn you cannot cast them.
card_roles.Skullclamp: One mana, and every 1/1 you own becomes two cards. With Bitterblossom, Nest of Scarabs and Grave Titan all making bodies, equip it the moment you have a token you are happy to kill.
card_roles.Deadly Dispute: Instant-speed conversion: a creature already in the removal crosshairs becomes two cards and a Treasure. Cast it in response to the removal, never before.
card_roles.Plumb the Forbidden: Your insurance against a wrath or a targeted exile — sacrifice as many creatures as you like in response and copy it for each. Keep two mana up any turn a sweeper is live.
card_roles.Sinister Gnarlbark: A card and a free counter at every end step, which with the Nest out is a free Insect every turn as well. Three mana for ignition you never have to pay for again.
card_roles.Insatiable Avarice: Three mana either way — one mode sets the top of your library, the other draws three for 3 life — and five mana buys both on one cast. Take the tutor mode when you are a piece short and both when you are short and out of cards.
card_roles.Demonic Tutor: Two mana, any card, straight to hand. When a kill is one piece short this is the shortest road there — do not spend it on a land.
card_roles.Vampiric Tutor: One mana at instant speed for the exact card you need, on top of your library. Cast it at the end of the turn before you need it, because it costs you a draw step.
card_roles.Beseech the Mirror: Bargain something you were going to sacrifice anyway and the four-or-less piece arrives free. Hold this one for the turn you want the tutor and the kill to happen together.
card_roles.Diabolic Intent: The additional cost is a creature dying, which every payoff on your board is already waiting for. Sacrifice into your drains and you get the tutor at a discount you were collecting anyway.
card_roles.Persist: Two mana returns a nonlegendary body carrying a counter — a creature and an Insect on one card when the Nest is out. Point it at something worth more than the counter takes off it.
card_roles.Victimize: One sacrifice, two bodies back tapped. It pays every layer at once: a death trigger going out and two arrivals coming in.
card_roles.Animate Dead: Two mana for the best creature in any graveyard, theirs included. The -1/-0 never matters when the body's job is to die again.
card_roles.Phyrexian Reclamation: Two mana and 2 life, at instant speed, as often as you like — this is how you rebuild through hate aimed at the battlefield. Buy the answered piece back on their end step.
card_roles.Mikaeus, the Unhallowed: Six mana turns every non-Human you own into a body that comes back, and beside the commander that alternation is a kill. Cast him when you can still hold something up, because the loop itself asks for no more mana.
card_roles.Massacre Girl, Known Killer: Wither makes your combat damage into counters, which is removal, ignition and Nest fuel from one attack step. Every small creature an opponent loses draws you a card on top of it.
card_roles.Skinrender: Three counters on arrival: kill their creature outright, or aim it at your own body and collect three Insects. Choose by what the board is short of, and it is usually bodies.
card_roles.Soul Snuffers: A counter on every creature sweeps the small stuff and lights the Nest across your whole board in one cast. Yes, it hits yours — that is normally why you are casting it.
card_roles.Fume Spitter: One mana, sacrifices itself, places a counter — the cheapest ignition you own and a death trigger in the same card. Play it turn one when the alternative is nothing.
card_roles.Black Sun's Zenith: The only sweeper you have that leaves counters behind, which makes it the only sweeper the Nest can see. Set X to what kills their board and let your drains collect on yours.
card_roles.Toxic Deluge: Three mana and X life clears anything, indestructible included. It hands out -X/-X rather than counters, so file it as your answer and never as your engine.
card_roles.Feed the Swarm: The one card in the 99 that destroys a noncreature permanent an opponent controls, and it only reaches enchantments. Hold it for the permanent that genuinely stops you rather than the first irritating thing you see.
card_roles.Deadly Rollick: Free while your commander is on the battlefield, and it exiles rather than destroys. This is the best argument for keeping Yawgmoth around on the turns you are not using him.
card_roles.Snuff Out: Instant-speed removal for four life and no mana, which is how you interact on a turn you spent assembling. It cannot touch a black creature, so check the table before you count on it.
card_roles.Fatal Push: One mana kills a two-drop, or a four-drop the moment anything of yours has left the battlefield this turn. In this deck that condition is on every turn — sacrifice something first and swing the ceiling up.
card_roles.Lightning Greaves: Zero equip pulls a piece out of the crosshairs and lets an outlet work the turn it lands. Move the boots off before you need to target that creature yourself.
card_roles.Supernatural Stamina: One mana saves a creature from removal and hands you a free death trigger on the way through. Keep it up on any turn your drain is out and the table has mana open.
card_roles.Gray Merchant of Asphodel: Count your devotion before you cast him and pick the turn the table is already low — in a list this full of black pips the number gets ugly fast. He is a Zombie for Gravecrawler and a reanimation target besides.
card_roles.Sol Ring: Two colorless on turn one is why your commander sometimes arrives on turn two. Play it the moment you see it and never think about it again.
card_roles.Ancient Tomb: Two mana out of a land for 2 damage a tap. Colorless is a genuine constraint here, so spend it on the generic half of a cost and leave the pips to a Swamp.
card_roles.Arcane Signet: Two mana, then black every turn after — unglamorous, and often the difference between a turn-3 and a turn-4 commander. Cast it on the turn it accelerates something, not on autopilot.
card_roles.Dark Ritual: One black into three, once. Spend it on the turn that changes the game — a turn-one Bitterblossom, a turn-two commander — and never on a turn you were merely ahead anyway.
card_roles.Castle Locthwain: Untapped black as long as you control a Swamp, which here is nearly always. Its draw costs life equal to your hand size, so fire it when your hand is almost empty.
card_roles.Cabal Pit: Black mana for a point of damage, and once your graveyard is seven deep it sacrifices itself to shrink a creature. Hold that mode for a blocker you actually need gone.
card_roles.Ifnir Deadlands: Black mana for a life, plus a late-game sink that drops two counters on an opposing creature. That is removal and Nest ignition out of a land slot — keep the Desert around to pay for it.
card_roles.Cabal Coffers: Two mana and a tap for a black per Swamp, which with 22 basics and Urborg out is the biggest tap you will make all game. It counts as one source on paper; play it like several.
card_roles.Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth: It makes no mana itself and counts for nothing in the source column — what it does is turn every land you own into a Swamp for Cabal Coffers and Snuff Out. Get it down early and let the rest of the base improve.
card_roles.Bojuka Bog: A tapped land that exiles a graveyard on arrival. Hold it for the reanimator seat instead of jamming it turn one; a tapped land costs you almost nothing on turn six.
card_roles.Takenuma, Abandoned Mire: Black mana, or channel it away to buy a creature back — cheaper for every legendary creature you control, and you run nine of them. A land that doubles as a recursion spell.
card_roles.Command Tower: Untapped black, no condition, no cost. Nothing here to think about.
card_roles.Exotic Orchard: It taps for whatever an opponent's lands could make, which is black often enough to count on. Glance at the table before you build a triple-black turn around it.
card_roles.City of Brass: Any colour, untapped, a point of damage a tap. In a deck whose kills finish at 80 life you will pay that all game and smile.
card_roles.Survivors' Encampment: Colorless, or any colour by tapping a spare body, and you generally have one. Tap the creature you were not planning to sacrifice this turn.
card_roles.Path of Ancestry: Enters tapped for black, and scries whenever that mana casts a Human or a Cleric. Put it down on a turn you were not going to spend all your mana anyway — with only three taplands in the base, that turn always comes.
card_roles.Agadeem's Awakening // Agadeem, the Unde: Pay the 3 life to have the land side arrive untapped; here that is almost always right. Keep the front face in mind for the turn after a wipe, when it brings your whole curve back at once.
card_roles.Malakir Rebirth // Malakir Mire: A land on the turns you are short and a two-life save on the turn your key creature gets targeted. The return is another death trigger for every drain you have out.
card_roles.Swamp: Twenty-two of them, which is why your black count works and why Cabal Coffers and Snuff Out do what they do. Lead on a basic and keep the utility lands for turns you can afford to spend on them.

mulligan:
Most people mulligan this deck hunting for the commander. Don't. He lands on turn four in 7,220 of 10,000 goldfished games with no help at all, and three of your four verified kills never name him — so keep the hand that gives him something to eat, or the hand that wins without him.

Keep a shape, not a card list: something that sacrifices, something to sacrifice, and two to four lands. That is what 9,192 of 10,000 kept hands look like, and from there your turn-3 land drop hits 91.9%.

The outlet and the fodder are interchangeable, so stop holding out for the good one. Carrion Feeder, Viscera Seer, Woe Strider, Yahenni and Blasting Station all do the outlet job. Bitterblossom, Reassembling Skeleton, Stitcher's Supplier and Gravecrawler are every one of them fodder. A free outlet turns up by turn 10 in 77.9% of games — you do not need the specific one in your opener.

Ship the hand that is all payoff, however good it looks. Exquisite Blood, Grave Titan and five lands is a mulligan: mean available mana is 3.911 on turn 4, so a five-drop with nothing under it means you do nothing for half the game. Enablers dig toward payoffs. Payoffs sit there waiting for an engine nobody built.

One land is a ship unless Sol Ring, Ancient Tomb or Dark Ritual is sitting next to it. Zero lands is always a ship, and only 288 opening sevens in 10,000 come out that way, so it will hardly ever be the decision in front of you.

Ship freely in general — you keep the first seven 81.8% of the time at a mean of 0.216 mulligans, which makes the first one a trade you are allowed to take on instinct. And take the hand with a tutor over the hand with the commander every time: a tutor is what turns a 6.9% kill into a 42.5% one.
upgrades:
Two answered classes out of five. That one figure buys almost every slot below it.

Thirteen removal copies sit above Walser's 8-10 floor, so depth is not the problem — across all seventy-nine maindeck entries, exactly one card destroys or exiles a noncreature permanent an opponent controls, and Feed the Swarm reaches enchantments only. Artifact and land are not thin here. They are zero.

Seven of the ten answer that, and they answer it from four different price points. Gate to Phyrexia is two mana and repeats every upkeep; Phyrexian Tribute is three mana, once; Meteor Golem is seven and reaches any nonland permanent at all; Nevinyrral's Disk is the one wipe in this colour identity that takes artifacts and enchantments alongside the board, against four sweepers already in the 99 that only kill creatures. Withering Torment is the instant-speed second copy of the card the deck already has, drawn 17.3% of the time by turn ten.

Two of those seven come out of the land slots instead of the spell slots, which is the cheapest breadth on the page. Strip Mine and Blast Zone leave the count at thirty-six land copies before and thirty-six after. Blast Zone matters at exactly one charge counter, because Grafdigger's Cage is mana value one and so are a lot of things that lock this deck. Climbing to mana value two costs {X}{X} and a whole extra turn.

The hole has a shape, and the shape is a small colourless permanent. Three of the four checker-passed kills read — from oracle text — as stopping under a static graveyard lock, so seven of these ten are ranked against an interaction nobody has put through the checker. That is the single biggest lever on this page's ordering, and it costs one stack scenario to settle.

Two more widen the kill that survives that lock rather than answering it. The Exquisite Blood line is 6.9% unassisted by turn ten and 42.5% with a tutor, mean turn 5.3, and the Blood half of it is one card against three partners — Bloodthirsty Conqueror makes that two against three. Pawn of Ulamog joins engine mana, the thinnest enabler group at 61.9%, against a drain at 82.4%, an outlet at 77.9% and fodder at 73.6%. That gap is where a body is worth more than a spell.

The tenth, Walking Ballista, closes nothing the audit named, and the page says so in its own entry. Every bracket figure was recomputed rather than asserted: the floor is 4 before and 4 after, on all ten, so nothing here changes the Rule 0 conversation. Three natural cuts are named — Supernatural Stamina, Toxic Deluge, Survivors' Encampment — and they are independent one-for-one proposals, not a package. And not one combo line these open is verified; each carries "needs a stack scenario", which is a bill, not a footnote.
mana_base:
Thirty-six land copies across 15 entries, and three of them enter tapped — only two of those always. Twenty-two are basic Swamps, so 61% of the mana base is a single card repeated. That concentration is exactly why Cabal Coffers counts as one source in the audit and behaves like something else entirely at the table.

Pip share and source share both read 1.0. They agree perfectly because there is only one colour here to disagree about, so there is nothing to reconcile — just a count. 34 black land sources against a target of 36, and the whole gap is the two lands that make no black at all: Ancient Tomb taps for {C}{C}, Urborg taps for nothing. The audit puts the caveat plainly, and it is worth quoting: “the target is a yardstick, not a possibility, in a 36-land deck”.

Nonland producers carry 34 up to 42, and the composition matters far more than the total. Ten cards file as ramp; eight of them add black. Sol Ring and Ashnod's Altar add {C}{C} apiece and no black whatsoever, and of the eight that do add it, only Arcane Signet taps for black unconditionally — Phyrexian Altar, Pitiless Plunderer and Warren Soultrader all want a creature to die first, and two of the four rituals are the back faces of lands. So read the jump from 88.2% on lands alone to 95.5% with the rocks and dorks as just over seven points bought largely on credit; the model takes no survival discount on the creatures underwriting it.

The demand side is mild for a mono-colour deck. 75 black pips spread across 55 cards, a maximum of 3 on any one card and an effective 2, with the first pip due on turn 1. Double black on curve is what this base is actually being asked for, and 34 land sources is comfortably more than that costs.

Development agrees. The land drop hits 99.7% on turn 2, 91.9% on turn 3, 80.8% on turn 4 and 58.8% by turn 6, with mean available mana of 3.082, 3.911 and 5.223 on those same turns against a commander that costs four and lands on a median turn 4. Nothing here is ever stuck on colour, and the mana is not the number in this deck worth worrying about.
threat_assessment:
The table has already decided what you are. You are the Yawgmoth deck: kill the commander, and the problem goes away. Let them keep believing it — it is wrong, and it is the most useful thing you own.

Three of your four verified kills never put him on the board. Stacks 009, 011 and 012 do not name him anywhere. So cast him on curve, draw four or five cards with him, and be visibly pleased when somebody spends removal.

He shows up on turn four in 7,220 of 10,000 goldfished games. Stop holding mana to protect him and stop mulliganing toward him — keep the hand that gives him something to eat instead.

Now take apart the other thing they believe. They are counting your creatures. Goldfish has you at 3.903 bodies by turn six, which reads as a fair little swarm, so keep casting them. The swarm is the costume, not the plan.

Two of your boards look like a kill and are not, and both are worth showing off. Yawgmoth with Nest of Scarabs and Bastion of Remembrance drains seven times and takes 28 life from a pod of 160, leaving every seat at 33 (stack 002). Swap Mirkwood Bats in and it is 13 per opponent, 52 across the table — and nobody dies (stack 008).

Price those boards as threats out loud and let the table answer them. Every removal spell spent on your value engine is one nobody is holding on the turn you assemble something real.

Which brings you to the game you will actually play most. Your engine layers turn up constantly and your kills do not: by turn ten you hold a drain 82.4% of the time, a free sacrifice outlet 77.9%, renewable fodder 73.6%, an ignition source 73.1% — against kill rates of 1.1%, 0.5%, 6.9% and 4.6%. Read that gap as a job description, not a disappointment.

The job is to be the seat the table needs alive. Sacrifice at instant speed on other people's turns and draw off it; the ability costs no mana at all, so it runs under a Sphere and through a lock.

Point the counters at opponents' creatures, never your own, whenever a legal target exists. Stack 002 measured an opposing two-toughness body extending the engine by two activations rather than ending it — free removal and free fuel in the same habit.

Put Grave Pact down and every activation becomes a table-wide edict. Sell that to whichever seat is being attacked, and charge for it.

Then spend your actual turns on one thing: finding the missing card. A tutor carries the Exquisite Blood kill from 6.9% to 42.5% and the Mikaeus kill from 4.6% to 33.7%, so never cast one for value. You are not digging for a good card. You are digging for the fourth corner of a configuration.

One card is doing far more than the table can see, and you have to stop misreading it too. Gravecrawler recasts itself from the graveyard for a single black while a Zombie is out, and that permission is the entire reason stacks 009 and 011 never end. It looks like a one-mana 2/1 in a deck full of one-mana 2/1s — play it turn one and expect nobody to touch it. Never feed it to the commander for a card; that trades a kill for a draw step.

Bastion of Remembrance is the drain three of the four kills route through, and it is the piece you cannot protect. Lightning Greaves, Supernatural Stamina and Malakir Rebirth all save a creature; Bastion is an enchantment. Hold it in hand until the turn it converts, and lead with literally anything else.

Here is exactly when you stop being ignored. Not when your board gets wide — when a second noncreature payoff hits the table. Exquisite Blood resolving, Phyrexian Altar landing beside a Gravecrawler, Mikaeus untapping. Mikaeus is the loudest of them, sitting in seven of the eleven two-card infinite records the bracket floor counts.

So let Mikaeus be the lightning rod, and deploy him on a turn you want removal spent. He is attached to your slowest line anyway — the one needing 39 activations against the 59 your own library permits (stack 010). Put the cheap half of a configuration down early and the loud half at the end step before your turn, when their mana is already gone.

Now the threat read that runs the other way, and it is the one this deck gets wrong. You do not fear spells. You fear permanents, and three of them in particular.

Grafdigger's Cage, Null Rod and Cursed Totem each switch off part of this machine, and not one card in the 99 destroys or exiles an artifact. Feed the Swarm reads creature or enchantment. That is the whole answer set, so plan around the hole rather than for it.

Learn which kill survives which, because one of them always does. Cage stops the Gravecrawler recasts, so both unbounded loops go with it and Exquisite Blood is what you have left. Null Rod takes Phyrexian Altar and the Treasure your Soultrader loop sacrifices for mana, and leaves you Mikaeus and Exquisite Blood. Cursed Totem takes the commander, Warren Soultrader and every creature outlet you own, and leaves the Phyrexian Altar loop, which does its sacrificing with an artifact.

So when one of those resolves, do not go shopping for an answer you do not have. Switch shapes that turn and tutor for the kill that still works. The resource-denial school puts the discipline exactly: "Name your outs early — the removal or velocity that breaks the piece that beats *you*, not the scariest piece" (strategy:threat-assessment.resource-denial).

And use the table, because you are the seat that cannot break an artifact. That makes somebody else's artifact removal the one thing worth buying with real currency — offer your spot removal, your edicts and your silence to whoever can break it, and overpay. It is cheaper than the game you lose staring at a permanent you cannot touch.

Expect your quiet to be discounted while you do all this. Krell's warning is your own playbook read backwards: "combo decks look non-threatening while advancing in secret, which is exactly why experienced tables hit the quiet ramp player" (strategy:multiplayer.threat-deflection). So never claim you have done nothing. Claim the board they can see, the seven-drain value engine, and let that be the thing they price.

At Rule 0, say it straight — honesty costs you nothing here and buys real goodwill. Bracket floor 4, forced by four Game Changers and by eleven two-card infinite records. Then say the part that matters: four rules-verified kills, two of them unbounded, every one of them taking all four opponents to zero at the same moment.

That last sentence is not flavour, it is your go decision. You never get a turn where you are lethal on one seat and merely frightening to the rest, so stop asking whether you can kill somebody and start asking whether what you hold is one of the four shapes. Count the table's open mana, assume every held answer appears, and then go. Stack 009 dips you to 39 life and refunds it; stack 011 costs nothing at all and gains you a life a lap. Those two you may attempt into a live table and still have a deck afterwards.
matchups:
Assign your seat before you assign your plan, and re-ask it every time the board turns over. Against fair decks you own the long game and you should act like it. Against anything assembling a lock or a clock faster than you assemble, you are the beatdown and the polite value plan is how you lose.

FAIR MIDRANGE is the table you will sit at most often, and it is the one where your engine runs for six turns without a kill in sight. Do not treat that as waiting. Sacrifice on their end steps, draw off it, aim the counters at their creatures, and let Grave Pact turn every activation into an edict nobody else at the table can produce.

Be the most useful neighbour in the pod while you dig. You hold a drain 82.4% of the time by turn ten and a free outlet 77.9%, so the machine is almost always there — the missing piece is what you spend turns on. Trade removal for goodwill, keep the aggressive seat pointed elsewhere, and cast a tutor only when it completes a shape.

SWEEPER CONTROL is holding a wrath with your name on it. Invite it.

Bastion of Remembrance, Zulaport Cutthroat and The Meathook Massacre each bill every opponent when a creature you control dies, and Blood Artist bills a chosen seat whenever any creature dies at all. Deploy fodder freely into open mana; their sweeper pays you four ways for every body it takes.

Rebuild structurally rather than from your hand. Reassembling Skeleton returns for two mana forever, Gravecrawler for one while a Zombie is out, and Bitterblossom makes a body a turn without spending a card — so never hold a creature back out of respect for a wrath.

Better still, a wrath touches none of your kills. Bastion, Exquisite Blood and Phyrexian Altar are all noncreature permanents, so keep the creature half of a configuration on the table and the noncreature half in your hand until the turn it converts.

Plumb the Forbidden is what flips this matchup outright. Assume a control seat that untaps with four or more open is holding the sweeper, and hold two mana whenever they do — their announcement becomes your draw step and every sacrifice fires whatever drain you already have down.

STAX AND TAX thinks it is slowing you down. Recount your hand rather than your board and you will see why it mostly is not.

Three of your four kills need essentially no external mana once assembled. Stack 009's Treasure exactly funds the next cast, stack 011's Phyrexian Altar refunds its own black every iteration, and stack 012 spends nothing at all. Your commander's ability costs no mana either, so keep activating it under a tax that has stopped everyone else.

Your window of weakness is deployment, not operation — so deploy under the tax as if this were the last turn you get to, and stop holding pieces back for a cleaner sequence that is not coming.

Against a Cursed Totem or a Pithing Needle pointed at your commander, pivot immediately to the Phyrexian Altar loop, which sacrifices with an artifact and never needs a creature's ability. Against a lock you cannot break, race it: tutor for Exquisite Blood, your fastest shape at a mean assembly turn of 5.301.

COMBO is your worst seat, so meet it head-on instead of hedging. You have no counterspells, and your instant-speed answers are Deadly Rollick, Fatal Push and Snuff Out — all pointed at creatures, against a kill that may never use one.

Spend them on the enabler the turn it lands, not at some ideal later moment. Deadly Rollick is free while you control your commander, which is most turns from four onward, and Snuff Out is free with a Swamp, which is always. The answer-economy school is blunt about the exception you are living in: "held answers rot — against combo, or lethal already on board, the last profitable moment is now" (strategy:threat-assessment.answer-economy).

Then race with the shape you can finish rather than the one you would prefer. Exquisite Blood assembles at 6.9% by turn ten unassisted and 42.5% with a tutor, faster than either recursion kill at 1.1% and 0.5%, so point every search at that pair. One caution to carry: stack 012 verified the loop with South Wind Avatar, whose own death trigger gains the life that ignites it. Marauding Blight-Priest and Starscape Cleric carry the same drain text and gain no life themselves, so line up an external lifegain event before you count on them.

AGGRO thinks a wide board and your 40 life are pressure. They are feeding you.

Four sweepers, 28 bodies to chump or eat, and Grave Pact converting your own engine into a table-wide edict make this your most comfortable seat. Choose the sweeper by what you want back: Black Sun's Zenith puts actual counters on each creature and your Nest of Scarabs reads exactly that, while Toxic Deluge and The Meathook Massacre hand out -X/-X and place nothing — so cast Zenith when you want bodies out of the wipe and Deluge when you simply want the board gone.

Spend life early and freely. Stack 011 leaves you at 80 and stack 012 gains you 40, so Necropotence, Bitterblossom, Black Market Connections and City of Brass are cheap now and expensive later. Switch from spending to defending one turn before it matters, not one after.

GRAVEYARD HATE deserves its own read, because it hits this deck unevenly and knowing which half is live is worth a whole game. Both unbounded kills cast Gravecrawler out of the graveyard on every single iteration, so a Rest in Peace effect blanks stacks 009 and 011 outright.

Stack 012 is the shape that survives, and its verified board holds an empty graveyard — so under hate, abandon the recursion plan on the spot and tutor for Exquisite Blood plus a body reading "whenever you gain life, each opponent loses 1 life."

Do not treat Mikaeus as a safe harbour on the way there. Undying brings the card back from your graveyard, so a permanent that seals or empties it is aimed at that line too, and nothing verified settles the interaction. Plan for the Exquisite Blood shape and let the Mikaeus line be a bonus if it survives.

You are not defenceless against their graveyard either. Bojuka Bog exiles one as it enters, off a land drop that costs you nothing — so hold it for the turn it strips a reanimation target rather than playing it the turn it is convenient.
